title: Nonlinear Equations and Systems, Part 3: Traps and the Fast Way

beats.say: In this video, we look at five mistakes students make with nonlinear equations, and then use Desmos to find solutions, count the solutions of a system, and find a constant with a slider.
Each trap is shown as a wrong line first, then the right line, with the reason it is so tempting.

scenes.title: Trap 1: the sign of a root

beats.say: Trap one. When you read solutions from factors, the sign flips. The factor x plus five equals zero when x is negative five. Students read the number as it appears.
Set each factor equal to zero and solve. x plus five equals zero gives x equals negative five, and x minus two equals zero gives x equals two.
Trap two. The equation x squared equals twenty-five has two solutions. Students take the square root and forget the negative one.
Both five and negative five square to twenty-five. Unless the question restricts x to be positive, both are solutions.
Trap three. After squaring, the radical equation gave x equals two and x equals nine. Students report both without checking.
Substituting x equals two gives a square root of nine on the left, which is three, and negative three on the right. That fails. Only nine works.
Trap four. In the hard problem, k squared equals sixty-four gives k equals plus or minus eight. The question asked for the positive value of k, but a student lists both.
beats.wrong_why: Only the positive value was asked

beats.say: Always re-read the question before answering. It asked for the positive value of k, so the answer is eight.
Trap five. For two x squared minus four x plus five, b is negative four, and c is five. Students sometimes add the product four a c instead of subtracting it.
The discriminant is b squared minus four a c. Sixteen minus forty is negative twenty-four, so there are no real solutions.
Desmos is often the fastest route. To solve an equation, graph the expression equal to zero and click the x-intercepts. Let us try x squared minus x minus twelve.
We type the left side minus the right side, so the solutions become the places where the graph meets the x axis.
Type y equals x, the caret key and a two, the right arrow, then minus x minus twelve.
Click the parabola, and then click the grey dot on the right. Desmos shows four comma zero.
Now click the grey dot on the left. Desmos shows negative three comma zero. So the solutions are four and negative three, matching our algebra.
To count the solutions of a system with a line and a parabola, graph both and count the intersections. Our system is y equals x squared minus four, and y equals two x minus five.
We type each equation and look at how the two graphs meet.
Type y equals x squared minus four. Remember the right arrow after the exponent.
Now type y equals two x minus five. The line seems to just touch the parabola.
Click the meeting point. Desmos shows one comma negative three, and there is only one point. So the system has exactly one solution, because the line is tangent to the parabola.
To find a constant, replace it with a slider. For x squared minus k x plus sixteen, we want the value of k where the parabola touches the x axis exactly once.

card.sub: Slide k until it touches once

beats.say: We graph the parabola with k as a slider, and then drag until the graph does what the question describes.
Type y equals x, the caret key and a two, the right arrow, then minus k x plus sixteen. Desmos creates a slider for k.
Drag k downward from twelve. The parabola crosses the x axis twice, then touches it once, and then rises above it.
The parabola touches the x axis exactly once when k equals eight. That matches the discriminant method, and the positive value is eight.
Now a practice problem. Solve x squared plus two x minus fifteen equals zero. Pause the video, try it, and then watch the solution.
We need two numbers that multiply to negative fifteen and add to positive two. Those are five and negative three.
Write the factors using those numbers. x plus five, times x minus three, equals zero.
Set each factor to zero. x plus five equals zero gives negative five, and x minus three equals zero gives three.
Check negative five. Twenty-five minus ten minus fifteen is zero. Check three. Nine plus six minus fifteen is zero. Both solutions work.
To recap. Solve each factor for zero, remember the negative root, and check radical solutions.
Read what the question asks, and subtract four a c in the discriminant.
Use Desmos for x-intercepts, intersection counts, and sliders. In the next topic, we study nonlinear functions.
